# Nandivisālajātaka (Ja 28)
**ID:** Ja 28
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Nandivisālajātaka* (Ja 28) is a canonical narrative in the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon, located in the *Ekanipāta* [Fausböll 1877]. In the frame story set at Jetavana, the Buddha rebukes the group of six monks (*chabbaggiyā*) for verbally abusing and taunting other monks with the ten modes of abuse [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Explaining that harsh speech causes resentment even in animals, the Buddha recounts an event from a past life [SuttaCentral].
In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a powerful ox or bull named Nandivisāla, raised kindly by an impoverished brahmin [Anālayo 2012; Levman 2014]. Out of gratitude, the bull proposes that the brahmin wager a thousand pieces that his bull can draw one hundred loaded carts lashed together [SuttaCentral; Levman 2014]. However, when the brahmin publicly urges the bull by calling him a wretch and a rogue, Nandivisāla refuses to budge, causing the brahmin to lose the wager [SuttaCentral; Levman 2014]. When the remorseful brahmin later speaks to him with gentle affection, the bull willingly pulls the carts and wins back the lost money with profit [Burlingame 1921b; Levman 2014]. The moral verse emphasizes the power of speech: one should speak only pleasant words and never harsh language (*manuññam eva bhāseyya*), for sweet speech won the owner his heavy burden drawn and prosperity [Burlingame 1921b; Fausböll 1877]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the brahmin is identified as Ānanda and the bull Nandivisāla as the Buddha himself [Anālayo 2012; Fausböll 1877].
SuttaCentral and modern scholars identify a direct parallel to this narrative in the Vinaya Piṭaka's Suttavibhaṅga, serving as the origin story (*nidāna*) for Bhikkhu Pācittiya 2 on abusive language (Vin IV 6) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2012; Appleton 2010; Norman 1983]. At the conclusion of the Vinaya version, the Buddha explicitly remarks that even at that time insulting and deriding was displeasing to him (*tadāpi me, bhikkhave, amanāpā khumsanā vambhanā*) [Anālayo 2012]. In post-canonical literature, the story is cited in the Dhammapada commentary alongside the *Kaṇha Usabha Jātaka* during the account of the Twin Miracle [Burlingame 1921a; Burlingame 1921b]. DharmaNexus identifies no internal text-reuse matches or cross-language parallel alignments exceeding threshold [DharmaNexus].
